                                              PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                             §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                                            §               OF TEXAS


                   NRG ENERGY, INC.’S COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE
       NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule and

questions for comment by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT or Commission)

regarding a large load demand management service (Proposed Rule) to implement Public Utility

Regulatory Act (PURA) 1 § 39.170(b) adopted by the Texas Legislature through Senate Bill 6

(SB6) in the 89th Legislative Session. 2 NRG is the parent company of retail electric providers

(REPs) and power generation companies (PGCs) with long-standing experience in the competitive

electricity markets in Texas.

                                              I.       INTRODUCTION
       NRG generally supports the structure of the Large Load Demand Management Service

(LLDMS) in the Proposed Rule, which creates a framework for the Electric Reliability Council of

Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) to develop the technical specifications for a service that should incentivize

large loads to curtail to help prevent firm load shed. This proposed service is a critical part of the

protections the Legislature, through SB6, directed the PUCT and ERCOT to establish for

residential and other small customers as part of the integration of large loads in ERCOT. NRG

proposes some changes below related to the payment for the program, which NRG recommends

should be similar to the settlement mechanism used for Congestion Revenue Rights (CRRs)

funding (with predictable payments throughout the year). The intent of this recommendation is to




       1
           Tex. Util. Code §§ 11.001-66.016 (PURA).
       2
           89th Tex. Leg., R.S., Senate Bill 6, § 6 (effective June 20, 2025) (hereafter, SB6).
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


help create more financial certainty, and thus ability to appropriately hedge, for Retail Electric

Providers (REPs) and other Load Serving Entities (LSEs) related to the cost of this service.

        In addition, the Proposed Rule would also address the firm load shed provisions in PURA

§ 39.170(a), by effectively repeating, verbatim, the statutory language, which requires

development of a load shed protocol for certain large load customers. NRG understands that

provision (both in the statute and as repeated in the Proposed Rule) as applying only to “load,”

meaning a net withdrawal of power from the grid. Importantly, that provision should not be

implemented in a manner that would disincentivize or interfere with the development of new co-

located generation resources by large loads or private use networks for transmission-connected

customers. As noted by Governor Abbott, 3 data centers should be encouraged to bring their own

generation (BYOG) to the greatest extent possible. BYOG arrangements such as Withdrawal

Limited Private Use Networks (WLPUNs) 4 protect the public from reliability risks and escalating

costs. Data centers invest in co-located generation to remove their load from the ERCOT system

during grid emergencies to allow them to continue to operate just like co-generation facilities for

industrial consumers that have been developed in ERCOT for over 40 years.

        While NRG does not suggest specific changes to the Proposed Rule’s incorporation and

restatement of the provisions in PURA § 39.170(a), NRG recommends that the Commission clarify

2026) (“Details should include…any effort and progress to construct or procure on-site electric generation including
generation type, or other measures to reduce demand on the ERCOT grid”), available at:
https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-directs-comprehensive-data-center-audit.
        4
           WLPUNs, in particular, are subject to a maximum withdrawal limit from the ERCOT grid at all times (not
just during emergencies) until the transmission system can accommodate the full load. For transmission planning
purposes, the WLPUN is studied on a combined generation and load basis, such that the system is not planned to
accommodate the full load. ERCOT Protocols § 2 (defining “WLPUN” as “A Private Use Network that contains both
generation and at least one Large Load, with an established MW Withdrawal limit at a single Point of Interconnection
(POI) determined by a system-wide interconnection study conducted by ERCOT”), § 3.10.7.3.1(2) (requiring the QSE
to abide by the withdrawal limit); ERCOT Planning Guide §§ 9.3.2.2, 9.5.4(1) (treatment of WLPUNs in transmission
planning).



NRG COMMENTS RE: PROPOSED RULE                                                                             2
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


that, in implementing this provision, transmission and distribution utilities (TDUs), electric

cooperatives, and municipally owned utilities should direct firm load shed based on the net load

on the ERCOT system (if any) from a site containing large load co-located with new generation 5

consistent with the application and historical operation of private use networks.



                              II.      RESPONSES TO STAFF QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1:           Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling
                      entity representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT
                      to deploy but is subject to availability verification during the Large Load
                      Demand Management Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large
                      load customer that is available but not ultimately instructed to deploy
                      during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated some percentage of
                      the market clearing price for the large load customer’s availability to
                      reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an
                      appropriate payment to the large load customer for their availability
                      during the LLDMS obligation period?

        NRG Response: Yes, it is reasonable to compensate large loads for their availability (i.e.,

capacity) to reduce demand in advance of an emergency condition regardless of whether the

capacity was deployed or not, and NRG supports the structure of the availability payment in the

Proposed Rule. Providing a capacity payment in those circumstances would be consistent with the

compensation structure for Emergency Response Service (ERS) (and ancillary services), and

ERCOT could reduce the payment, like it does for ERS, for failure to satisfy availability and testing

requirements in the absence of any deployments. 6 A capacity payment effectively compensates the

large load for maintaining availability to deploy, which could entail some costs, as well as for

foregoing the opportunity to participate in other services that offer capacity payments, like ERS.



        5
          Large loads co-located with existing generation are subject to different statutory requirements related to
curtailment, as set out in PURA § 39.169 and the associated Commission orders related to net-metering arrangements.
        6
          See, e.g., ERCOT Protocols §§ 3.14.3.1, 6.6.11.1, 8.1.3.3; ERCOT Emergency Response Service, Technical
Requirements & Scope of Work (Jun. 1, 2026 – Sept. 30, 2026).



NRG COMMENTS RE: PROPOSED RULE                                                                             3
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


QUESTION 2:           Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a
                      calendar year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       NRG Response: The proposed budget of $54 million is a reasonable starting point given

the costs of other programs like Firm Fuel Supply Service (FFSS) (which currently also has a $54

million budget per obligation period 7) and ERS (which currently has a budget of $75 million per

year 8). The Commission can adjust the program budget up or down in the future depending on

participation levels and need.

QUESTION 3:           What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition
                      and how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure
                      LLDMS?

       NRG Response: NRG supports the procurement and deployment framework in the

Proposed Rule, which includes a pre-qualification process and event-specific procurement and

deployment. Using an event-specific procurement and deployment process will allow ERCOT to

more accurately assess the reliability risk and right-size the procurement amount to avoid excess

costs. ERCOT should be provided with discretion to procure the LLDMS well in advance of a

reliability event as well as to deploy the service prior to emergency conditions on the ERCOT

system. NRG further supports the approach of the Proposed Rule to set basic parameters (similar

to the rules for ERS 9 and FFSS 10) and leave the technical details for further development in the

ERCOT stakeholder process.

QUESTION 4:           Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission
                      emergencies? If so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose
                      on this authority?

         NRG Response: Yes. The growth of large loads could impact reliability on the transmission

system as well as resource adequacy and the LLDMS should be available to ERCOT as a tool to

address both. The LLDMS could help ERCOT avoid transmission emergencies such as potential

Interconnection Reliability Operating Limit (IROL) violations as well as stability issues caused by

inadequate ride-through capabilities.


                            III.     COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED RULE

         A. Proposed Section 25.521(a) – Clarify Firm Load Shed for Transmission-Voltage
            Customers that Co-Locate with Generation

         As noted above, NRG understands the Proposed Rule language, which restates the statutory

language from PURA § 39.170(a), as applying a firm load shed requirement only to “load” that is

consuming electricity on a net basis from the grid. Importantly, NRG interprets this language to

maintain the status quo with respect to the historical operation of private use networks on the

ERCOT system, by not requiring a large load co-located with new generation 11 to curtail if the on-

site generation is serving the entire demand of the load.


         Applying basic tenets of statutory interpretation, 12 PURA §39.170(a) is best interpreted as

imposing firm load shed requirements only on large load customers that are consuming electricity


          11
             As noted, supra, in note 5, large loads that co-locate with existing generation resources are subject to
different requirements under SB6 (PURA § 39.169) and associated Commission orders. E.g., Application of Freestone
Power Generation, LLC and C1 Freestone 1 LLC for Approval of a Net Metering Arrangement, Docket No. 58872,
Order (May 7, 2026), Application for Crusoe Energy Systems LLC, FGE Goodnight I, LLC and Ensign Infrastructure
LLC for Approval of a Net Metering Arrangement, Docket No. 58881, Order (Apr. 23, 2026), and Application of
Crusoe Energy Systems LLC, FGE Goodnight I, LLC and Ensign Infrastructure LLC for Approval of a Net Metering
Arrangement, Docket No. 59220, Order (Jul. 24, 2026).
         12
            See, e.g., Tex. Gov’t Code § 311.011 (statutory words and phrases should be construed in context and
according to the rules of grammar and common usage, and terms that have acquired a technical meaning shall be
interpreted according to that meaning); id. § 311.023 (in construing a statute, a court may consider the object to be


NRG COMMENTS RE: PROPOSED RULE                                                                             5
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


from the ERCOT system on a net basis during a grid emergency (and not from on-site generation).

This section of SB6 will ensure that large loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 participate

in firm load shed to help alleviate emergency conditions resulting from transmission security issues

or inadequate supply to meet system demand—i.e., so that new large loads will not be prioritized

over the average Texan during grid emergencies. However, many data center customers have

indicated a desire—consistent with recent directives by the Governor 13—to co-locate with new

generation in order to maximize reliability for their site and contribute to the reliability of the

ERCOT system by removing their load from the ERCOT grid during such emergencies, which

should help mitigate public concerns with both affordability and reliability. During a grid

emergency, if these large loads are consuming power only from on-site generation (and not the

ERCOT system), then these large loads should not be considered a “load” at all from the

perspective of the ERCOT grid and the application of PURA § 39.170(a), and thus should not be

required to curtail their consumption in order to make the on-site generation available to the grid. 14

Allowing these loads to continue consuming power from on-site generation during a grid

emergency would be consistent with the treatment of existing co-generation and private use

network arrangements developed over the past 40 years, which exceed 18,000MW. 15


         To incentivize and encourage these arrangements, and to implement the statute as written,

the Proposed Rule should be implemented by TDUs, municipally-owned utilities, and electric

         14
           ERCOT Protocols, Section 2 defines “load” as “energy in MWh delivered” at a “specified point” on the
“system.” Thus, to be load at all, there must be a delivery of energy from the ERCOT system to the site (i.e., the site
must be a net importer of electricity).

 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


cooperatives as applicable only to large loads that are consuming from the ERCOT system and

contributing to the emergency conditions, as intended by SB6. 16 If a large load customer is being

served by new co-located generation, which was likely funded by the large load customer for its

own use to help mitigate the impacts of these exact scenarios, and not consuming from the ERCOT

system, the customer’s off-grid load should not be subject to firm load shed.


         B. Proposed Section 25.521(f) – Funding Mechanism for the LLDMS

         NRG recommends that, rather than direct ERCOT to charge REPs and other LSEs for

LLDMS on a load-ratio share basis during the procurement period, the Proposed Rule should

establish a fund similar conceptually to the CRR Balancing Account, 17 in order to make the charge

more predictable for LSEs and thus better enable LSEs to enter hedging arrangements that cover

those costs. Under NRG’s proposal, ERCOT would charge LSEs a modest flat fixed charge to

accrue revenue in the fund over the course of the year until the fund reached the program budget.

As ERCOT procured the LLDMS, the fund would be drawn down by ERCOT to issue payments

to those awarded in the procurement. ERCOT would cease charging LSEs for the fund once it

reached the budget.


         NRG proposes rule language below to effectuate this recommendation:

requiring firm load shed of large loads co-located with new generation during a firm load shed event would also ignore
that SB6 only addresses the potential for curtailment requirements for co-locations with existing generation resources
(addressed in PURA § 39.169) and backup generation (addressed in PURA § 37.0561) and does not mention any such
requirements (or associated processes to impose such requirements) for co-locations with new generation resources.
See Project No. 58482, NRG Energy, Inc.’s Comments in Response to Staff’s Questions (Apr. 8, 2026).

              …


              (3) ERCOT must charge each load serving entity for LLDMS deployment costs

              based upon the LSE’s load ratio share during the procurement period issue the

              payments for the program from a rolling fund administered by ERCOT that accrues

              revenue up to the program budget in (4) below by accruing a fixed charge to all

              Load Serving Entities.


                                           CONCLUSION


       NRG appreciates the Commission’s consideration of its comments in response to the

Proposed Rule and associated questions regarding the large load demand management service, as

well as the requirements in PURA § 39.170(a), adopted via SB6 from the 89th Legislative Session.

                    NRG ENERGY, INC.’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

  •   NRG generally supports the proposed structure of the Large Load Demand Management
      Service (LLDMS) in the Proposed Rule, which creates a framework for the Electric
      Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) to develop the technical specifications for the
      service, which should incentivize large loads to curtail to help prevent firm load shed.
  •   This proposed service is a critical part of the protections the Legislature, through Senate
      Bill 6 (SB6), directed the PUCT and ERCOT to establish for residential and other small
      customers as part of the integration of large loads in ERCOT.
  •   NRG proposes some changes related to the payment for the program, which NRG
      recommends should be similar to the settlement mechanism used for Congestion Revenue
      Rights (CRRs) to create a more predictable charge throughout the year.
         o Specifically, ERCOT should create an account, funded throughout the year by Load
           Serving Entities (LSEs) through a small, predictable charge up to the program
           budget, and should draw down from the account to pay for LLDMS until the budget
           is exhausted.
         o The intent of this recommendation is to help create more financial certainty, and
           thus ability to appropriately hedge, for Retail Electric Providers and other LSEs
           related to the cost of this service.
  •   With respect to PURA § 39.170(a) (related to firm load shed for large loads), the Proposed
      Rule effectively repeats, verbatim, the statutory language, which requires development of
      a load shed protocol for certain large load customers.
  •   NRG understands that provision (both in the statute and as repeated in the Proposed Rule)
      as applying only to “load,” meaning a net withdrawal of power from the grid (and not a
      situation where a load is consuming power entirely from its on-site generation and not
      drawing any power from the grid on a net basis). This understanding is consistent with the
      treatment of private use networks (PUNs) developed in ERCOT over the past 40 years.
  •   Importantly, that provision should not be implemented in a manner that would
      disincentivize or interfere with the development of new co-located generation resources by
      large loads. This is consistent with Governor Abbott’s statements that data centers should
      be encouraged to bring their own generation (BYOG) to the greatest extent possible.
  •   With respect to the questions: (1) NRG supports the Proposed Rule’s availability payment
      and associated percentage for large loads that are available but not deployed (consistent
      with the availability payments provided for ancillary services and Emergency Response
      Service (ERS)); (2) NRG supports the proposed $54 million budget as consistent with
      similar programs like ERS and Firm Fuel Supply Service, and the Commission could adjust
      the budget in the future if warranted based on participation levels and need; (3) NRG
      supports the procurement and deployment framework in the Proposed Rule, which includes
      a pre-qualification process and event-specific procurement and deployment; and (4) NRG
      supports the use of LLDMS for transmission emergencies in addition to extreme weather.

This section of SB6 will ensure that large loads interconnected after December 31, 2025 participate

in firm load shed to help alleviate emergency conditions resulting from transmission security issues

or inadequate supply to meet system demand-i.e., so that new large loads will not be prioritized

over the average Texan during grid emergencies. However, many data center customers have

indicated a desire--consistent with recent directives by the Governorl3_to co-locate with new

generation in order to maximize reliability for their site and contribute to the reliability of the

ERCOT system by removing their load from the ERCOT grid during such emergencies, which

should help mitigate public concerns with both affordability and reliability. During a grid

emergency, if these large loads are consuming power only from on-site generation (and not the

ERCOT system), then these large loads should not be considered a "load" at all from the

perspective of the ERCOT grid and the application of PURA § 39.170(a), and thus should not be

required to curtail their consumption in order to make the on-site generation available to the grid. 14

Allowing these loads to continue consuming power from on-site generation during a grid

emergency would be consistent with the treatment of existing co-generation and private use

network arrangements developed over the past 40 years, which exceed 18,000MW.15

         B. Proposed Section 25.521(f) - Funding Mechanism for the LLDMS

         NRG recommends that, rather than direct ERCOT to charge REPs and other LSEs for

LLDMS on a load-ratio share basis during the procurement period, the Proposed Rule should

establish a fund similar conceptually to the CRR Balancing Account,17 in order to make the charge

more predictable for LSEs and thus better enable LSEs to enter hedging arrangements that cover

those costs. Under NRG's proposal, ERCOT would charge LSEs a modest flat fixed charge to

accrue revenue in the fund over the course of the year until the fund reached the program budget.

As ERCOT procured the LLDMS, the fund would be drawn down by ERCOT to issue payments

to those awarded in the procurement. ERCOT would cease charging LSEs for the fund once it

reached the budget.

                    NRG ENERGY, INC.'S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

  •   NRG generally supports the proposed structure of the Large Load Demand Management
      Service (LLDMS) in the Proposed Rule, which creates a framework for the Electric
      Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) to develop the technical specifications for the
      service, which should incentivize large loads to curtail to help prevent firm load shed.
  •   This proposed service is a critical part of the protections the Legislature, through Senate
      Bill 6 (SB6), directed the PUCT and ERCOT to establish for residential and other small
      customers as part of the integration of large loads in ERCOT.
  •   NRG proposes some changes related to the payment for the program, which NRG
      recommends should be similar to the settlement mechanism used for Congestion Revenue
      Rights (CRRs) to create a more predictable charge throughout the year.
         o   Specifically, ERCOT should create an account, funded throughout the year by Load
             Serving Entities (LSEs) through a small, predictable charge up to the program
             budget, and should draw down from the account to pay for LLDMS until the budget
             is exhausted.
         o   The intent of this recommendation is to help create more financial certainty, and
             thus ability to appropriately hedge, for Retail Electric Providers and other LSEs
             related to the cost of this service.
  •   With respect to PURA § 39.170(a) (related to firm load shed for large loads), the Proposed
      Rule effectively repeats, verbatim, the statutory language, which requires development of
      a load shed protocol for certain large load customers.
  •   NRG understands that provision (both in the statute and as repeated in the Proposed Rule)
      as applying only to "load," meaning a net withdrawal of power from the grid (and not a
      situation where a load is consuming power entirely from its on-site generation and not
      drawing any power from the grid on a net basis). This understanding is consistent with the
      treatment of private use networks (FUNs) developed in ERCOT over the past 40 years.
  •   Importantly, that provision should not be implemented in a manner that would
      disincentivize or interfere with the development of new co-located generation resources by
      large loads. This is consistent with Governor Abbott's statements that data centers should
      be encouraged to bring their own generation (BYOG) to the greatest extent possible.
  •   With respect to the questions: (1) NRG supports the Proposed Rule's availability payment
      and associated percentage for large loads that are available but not deployed (consistent
      with the availability payments provided for ancillary services and Emergency Response
      Service (ERS)); (2) NRG supports the proposed $54 million budget as consistent with
      similar programs like ERS and Firm Fuel Supply Service, and the Commission could adjust
      the budget in the future if warranted based on participation levels and need; (3) NRG
      supports the procurement and deployment framework in the Proposed Rule, which includes
      a pre-qualification process and event-specific procurement and deployment; and (4) NRG
      supports the use of LLDMS for transmission emergencies in addition to extreme weather.
